name: Symphonia
baseline: FFmpeg libavcodec native decoders (FLAC, ALAC, MP1, MP2, MP3, AAC-LC, Vorbis, ADPCM), single-threaded, built as the static 'ffbench' example from a pdeljanov/FFmpeg fork
workload: Single-thread decode-only of one or two real audio files per codec (44.1/48/96 kHz), timed with hyperfine (30 runs after 3 warmups), on an Intel Core i7-4790K, an Apple M1 Pro and a Raspberry Pi 4B.
claimed_speedup: Relative decode time Symphonia/FFmpeg (below 1.0 means Symphonia is faster). i7-4790K: FLAC 0.71-0.74, ALAC 0.73-0.79, MP1 0.45-0.48, MP2 0.60, MP3 320 kbps 0.84, ADPCM IMA 0.83. M1 Pro: FLAC 0.51-0.64, ALAC 0.77-0.81, MP1 0.63-0.64, MP2 0.72-0.77, ADPCM MS 0.59, MP3 320 kbps 0.81. Raspberry Pi 4B: FLAC 0.96-1.04, ALAC 0.81-0.88, MP1 0.83-0.87, MP2 0.91-0.93. Slower than FFmpeg on AAC-LC (1.10-1.27), Vorbis (1.05-1.24) and MP3 128 kbps (1.00-1.07). The README summarises this as 'generally +/-15%' of FFmpeg.
compiler_and_flags: Symphonia built with rustc 1.67.0 and RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native', SIMD enabled. FFmpeg built with a plain './configure' (compiler version and flags not stated).
hardware: Intel Core i7-4790K 4C/8T @ 4.0 GHz; Apple M1 Pro (8 Firestorm + 2 Icestorm cores); Raspberry Pi 4B (Broadcom BCM2711, Cortex-A72 @ 1.5 GHz)
tradeoffs: Pure Rust audio decoding and demuxing library, no C API yet (listed as planned), so using it from C++ needs a hand-written FFI shim. Decode only, no encoders. Needs a recent rustc, and the README says performance depends strongly on compiler version because the decoders rely on auto-vectorization.
caveats: First-party results, so tier C: the test files come from the author's personal media library (not published) and only one or two files are used per codec, which the page itself says favours the decoders it was tuned on. The page was last updated 2023-02-03 (rustc 1.67.0, Symphonia main of that date), long before the current v0.6.1, so the numbers may be stale. The FFmpeg C compiler and flags are not stated. Results are mixed: Symphonia loses on AAC-LC and Vorbis everywhere and on most codecs on the Raspberry Pi, and wins mainly on FLAC, ALAC, MP1 and MP2. FFmpeg ran single-threaded (its FLAC/ALAC threading is not the default).
found_via: WebSearch 'Rust FLAC decoder faster than libFLAC benchmark claxon zune-flac symphonia ffmpeg decode speed' surfaced Symphonia/BENCHMARKS.md

name: rusty_flac
baseline: FFmpeg 8.1.2 native flac encoder and decoder (libavcodec)
workload: Single-core CPU-time comparison on a 180 s 44.1 kHz stereo music clip (guitar, piano, vocal): encode at -compression_level 8 and decode of an FFmpeg-encoded stream; pinned to one core, ABBA-alternated, 31 pairs, outputs verified lossless before timing.
claimed_speedup: Encode 672 ms vs 813 ms (0.83x FFmpeg CPU time, 17.3% faster); decode 266 ms vs 344 ms (0.77x, 22.7% faster); 31/31 wins on both, z = 5.57. Output files smaller than FFmpeg's on 20 of 20 gate-matrix combinations (for example stereo guitar s24 level 8: 539,087 vs 565,122 bytes).
hardware: Not stated ('single core, this machine'); four AVX2 kernels are runtime-detected
stars_or_usage: 1 star; README says 321 active installs via one named downstream app
tradeoffs: Pure Rust (no_std plus alloc capable, unsafe only in four AVX2 kernels with scalar twins), no C API, so C++ use needs an FFI shim. FLAC subset with LPC orders up to 12. Part of the Remade With Rust ecosystem, which also ships remade_ffmpeg_rs.
caveats: First-party claim: CPU model, compiler and rustc flags are not stated and the harness outputs are not published as raw data, so it falls short of tier A. The baseline is FFmpeg's native flac encoder, not the reference libFLAC; libFLAC was not tested. Single 180 s clip for the speed numbers; the smaller-file claim is on the gate matrix, not on the timed clip. Project is young and its commit history shows rapid release churn (v0.2.0 merged 2026-09-30).
found_via: WebSearch 'Rust FLAC decoder faster than libFLAC benchmark claxon zune-flac symphonia ffmpeg decode speed'

name: HALAC (High Availability Lossless Audio Compression)
baseline: FLAC 1.5.0 (libFLAC) -8 and -5; the same release notes also list WavPack 5.9.0 -h, Monkey's Audio and OptimFROG
workload: Single-thread encode and decode of six BipTunia albums, 24-bit 44.1 kHz stereo, about 5.88 GB, release 0.5.4 notes; a separate 29-song 32-bit float set (about 2 GB) in release 0.4.8 notes.
claimed_speedup: Release 0.5.4 (Ryzen 9 9600X, single thread): HALAC -plus encodes in 11.578 s and decodes in 13.201 s with 4,232,751,891 bytes, versus FLAC 1.5.0 -8 at 50.802 s encode, 14.357 s decode, 4,243,522,638 bytes (about 4.4x faster encode, 1.09x faster decode, slightly smaller output; derived from page data). HALAC -normal: 7.200 s encode, 9.353 s decode, 4,268,470,589 bytes versus FLAC -5 at 15.857 s, 13.451 s, 4,265,600,750 bytes (about 2.2x faster encode at equal size, derived from page data). Release 0.4.8 float set: HALAC normal 3.050 s encode / 4.290 s decode, 1,381,439,835 bytes, versus OptimFROG fast 39.310 s / 32.179 s, 1,346,477,460 bytes, and WavPack fast 20.675 s / 13.914 s, 1,392,225,168 bytes.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for 0.5.4 (0.4.8 notes say 'Single Thread, AVX2')
tradeoffs: Uses ANS (FSE) entropy coding instead of Rice coding, trading a few percent of compression for speed; OptimFROG compresses better. Releases cover 16/24-bit and 32-bit float PCM and up to 128 channels. No SIMD/GPU in early versions, AVX2 and multithreading added from 0.4.3.
caveats: First-party release notes with numbers but no benchmark script, compiler or flags, and the audio test sets are not distributed, so tier C. The source in the repository is only version 0.1.9 (halac_encode/decode_v.0.1.9 plus an FSE folder); the benchmarked 0.4.x-0.6.x builds are release assets, so the measured code may not be what the repo source builds. Release pages show dates without a year in the fetched text. The 0.5.4 notes do not say whether HALAC ran multi-threaded. The FLAC decode gap is small (1.09x); the headline win is encode speed. Baseline FLAC is not in this category's baseline list.
found_via: WebSearch 'HALAC lossless audio codec github faster than FLAC OptimFROG benchmark'

name: SuperFast Codecs (fre:ac multi-threaded codec drivers)
baseline: fre:ac's regular single-threaded codec drivers: libopus (Opus), FAAC and Core Audio AAC in the initial release; FDK-AAC, LAME and Speex drivers added later
workload: Converting a single input file to a single output file with 4 worker threads, each running its own codec instance on overlapping 128-frame blocks (8-frame overlap).
claimed_speedup: 'Using four threads, the conversion is already three times faster than with the regular drivers, which use only a single thread in this mode' (single file mode). In multi file mode the SuperFast drivers are only slightly faster. The measured chart is an image in the PDF; the text gives no per-codec table.
hardware: Not stated (the text mentions a 6 core CPU)
stars_or_usage: 65 stars; code merged into mainline fre:ac (BoCA)
tradeoffs: Chunked parallelism over several codec instances, so output is not bit-identical to a single-threaded encode and the 8/128 overlap caps speedup at 16x. Works for Opus, AAC, Speex and MP3 drivers; the author says Vorbis, FLAC and WMA do not fit. Needs the fre:ac BoCA and smooth class libraries to build. It speeds up a driver, not the codec library itself.
caveats: First-party blog post (PDF) whose numbers are only in a chart image; CPU, thread counts per test and codec versions are not given in text, so tier C. The comparison is multi-threaded drivers against the same codec run single-threaded, not a faster codec implementation. Repo is archived since 2020-12-11 (code lives on in enzo1982/BoCA). The Opus resampler in the pipeline stays single-threaded, which limits gains for non-48 kHz input.
found_via: WebFetch of github.com/topics/opus?l=c (superfast flagged as a speed project), then the repo README and doc/SuperFast Codecs.pdf

name: av2-turbo (AVM SYCL GPU acceleration)
baseline: AVM (AV2 reference encoder) CPU code paths; the benchmark table calls it only 'CPU Baseline' with no encoder, version or flags named
workload: SYCL/CUDA/OpenCL GPU kernels for DCT 8x8, SAD 16x16 motion estimation, loop filter and intra prediction, plus a 'full encoding pipeline' fps table at 720p, 1080p and 4K.
claimed_speedup: README: '3-5x real-world speedup on AV2 encoding'. docs/benchmarks.md: 1080p30 124 fps on RTX 4090 vs 28 fps 'CPU Baseline' (4.4x); 4K30 38 fps vs 8 fps (4.8x); 720p30 185 fps vs 45 fps (4.1x). Kernel rows: DCT 8x8 13.9x-31.4x, SAD 16x16 17.1x-24.0x, loop filter 11.1x-11.8x, intra 8x8 11.4x-12.0x.
compiler_and_flags: Intel DPC++ 2024.0, GCC 11.4, CUDA 12.2, NVIDIA driver 535.154.05, CMake Release build
hardware: Config A: Intel i9-13900K + NVIDIA RTX 4090 (24 GB); Config B: i7-12700K + RTX 3080; Config C: i7-12700K + Arc A770; Config D: Ryzen 9 7950X + RX 7900 XTX
tradeoffs: Needs a GPU and a SYCL toolchain (DPC++ or AdaptiveCpp). Batching is required because single-kernel launch overhead is 94% of a single DCT 8x8. AMD and ARM backends are marked in progress. License follows the AVM codebase (BSD 3-Clause Clear with the AOMedia patent license).
caveats: Very low confidence in the claim. The repository holds only SYCL kernels and wrappers, not an encoder, so the 'full encoding pipeline' fps figures cannot come from the repo's own code. The visible test results in the README are unit-test timings (for example DCT 8x8 average 50.14 us on an Intel Xeon Gold 6530 with OpenCL), not encoder runs. The CPU baseline is unnamed, no raw logs, CSV or CI output are published, and the fps figures look implausibly high for an AV2 reference-class encoder. No end-to-end comparison against an unmodified AVM encoder is given. Tier C only because numbers exist without a stated methodology; the verifier should check whether the data is real.
found_via: WebFetch of github.com/topics/hevc?l=c%2B%2B and topics/av1?l=c%2B%2B (only repo flagged with a speed claim), then WebSearch 'av2-turbo github AV2 encoder decoder faster than libaom benchmark'

name: libsoxr (SoX Resampler library)
baseline: libsamplerate (Secret Rabbit Code) 'sinc_best' through the Python 'samplerate' and 'scikits.samplerate' wrappers
workload: Resample a 2 s, 96,000-sample float64 mono log-sweep from 48 kHz to 44.1 kHz in Python with %timeit; soxr measured through the python-soxr binding with default settings.
claimed_speedup: soxr.resample 1.16 ms +/- 2.42 us per call versus samplerate sinc_best 76.8 ms +/- 1.03 ms and scikits.samplerate sinc_best 75.5 ms +/- 57.4 us, about 66x faster than samplerate (derived from page data). The same shootout lists scipy.signal.resample 2.42 ms, torchaudio 9.98-10 ms, resampy kaiser_fast 10.5 ms, resampy kaiser_best 44.8 ms, nnresample 16 ms, julius 16.2 ms.
stars_or_usage: 181 stars; widely packaged and bound from Python
tradeoffs: LGPL licence, a copyleft constraint for static linking. Throughput comes from large internal batches, so latency is high (the SampleRateTap comparison measures 8.8-16.4 ms for soxr HQ).
caveats: Independent third-party shootout (jonashaag/audio-resampling-in-python, last commit 2021-06-09) found as extra evidence for an already catalogued project. It measures the python-soxr and python-samplerate wrappers, not the C libraries directly; the notebook was run in a Colab-style environment with no CPU model stated, and quality settings are not matched (soxr defaults versus libsamplerate sinc_best, the slowest and highest-quality converter), so the ratio overstates a like-for-like gap. libsoxr's own repo has no commits since 2018-02-24.
found_via: WebSearch 'audio resampler benchmark libsamplerate soxr speexdsp zita-resampler comparison speed github repository results table'

name: go-flac
baseline: FFmpeg native flac encoder (libavcodec); the same README table also measures libFLAC and SoX, and libFLAC is faster than go-flac
workload: Encode at level 5, single-threaded, of a deterministic 30-minute mono 48 kHz/16-bit generated mix using scripts/bench-encoders.sh; plus a 2026-09-05 snapshot on real 48 kHz recordings at 16/24/32-bit.
claimed_speedup: Input MB/s on the default input: amd64 (i7-1260P) go-flac 147 vs ffmpeg 128 (about 1.15x, derived from page data), libFLAC 229, SoX 194; arm64 (Cortex-A76) go-flac 51 vs ffmpeg 48 (about 1.06x, derived), libFLAC 76. Real-recording snapshot: 16-bit about 19 ms vs about 71 ms, 24-bit about 25 ms vs about 61 ms for ffmpeg flac (machine not stated). README: 'libFLAC's reference encoder remains about 1.5x faster'.
hardware: Intel i7-1260P (amd64) and Cortex-A76 (arm64); machine for the real-recording snapshot not stated
tradeoffs: Pure Go with no cgo, SIMD kernels (AVX2 on amd64, NEON on arm64) bit-identical to the scalar fallback. Stays bit-exact at 32-bit where the README says ffmpeg's FLAC encoder truncates to 24-bit. Go only, so C++ callers would need a c-shared build or a rewrite.
caveats: First-party claim. The benchmark script is public and CPU models are given, but the Go version, the ffmpeg version and build, and compiler flags are not stated, so tier C. The win over ffmpeg is modest on the controlled input (1.06x-1.15x) and go-flac is clearly slower than libFLAC (about 1.5x). The README text says go-flac beats ffmpeg on ratio, but its own table lists ffmpeg at 0.8519 and go-flac at 0.8523 (lower is smaller). The 19 ms vs 71 ms snapshot is a small directional sample on an unstated machine. Young repo (commits visible from July 2026).
found_via: WebFetch of github.com/topics/flac-encoder (single result), then the repo README

name: zita-resampler
baseline: libsamplerate (Secret Rabbit Code), named in the library docs as the comparison
workload: No workload stated; the docs make a general CPU-load claim for real-time audio sample-rate conversion.
claimed_speedup: 'Even at the highest quality setting libzita-resampler will be faster than most similar libraries providing the same quality, e.g. libsamplerate.' Version 1.8.0 SSE2 build 'will reduce CPU load by a factor of at least 2'. No numbers beyond that.
stars_or_usage: 35 stars (GitHub copy); also listed as a resampler option in the SampleRateTap comparison doc
tradeoffs: GPL, so copyleft for linked code. Single-precision float only, interleaved multichannel, fixed-ratio Resampler plus variable-ratio VResampler class. Quality/CPU trade-off range of about 1:6.
caveats: Tier D: a first-party statement with no benchmark numbers. This GitHub repository is a 2021 copy (7 commits, Feb-Mar 2021) of the upstream 1.8.0 release by Fons Adriaensen, not the canonical source; the upstream site is not reachable from this environment so newer releases were not checked, which is why maintenance is 'unknown'. The SampleRateTap COMPARISON.md lists zita-resampler as having no published CI-verified figures.
found_via: WebSearch 'audio resampler benchmark libsamplerate soxr speexdsp zita-resampler comparison speed github repository results table'

name: libsoxr (SoX Resampler library)
workload: Time to convert generated RightMark test files (44.1, 48 and 96 kHz stereo, 16-bit integer or 32-bit float) to other rates with the speex and soxr command-line test harness, all files on tmpfs, real/user/system seconds.
claimed_speedup: Real seconds, 44.1 kHz 16-bit to 48 kHz: speex-10 4.35, speex-5 0.56, speex-1 0.23 versus soxr-vhq 0.29, soxr-hq 0.16, soxr-mq 0.15, soxr-lq 0.23. 48 kHz 16-bit to 44.1 kHz: speex-10 4.32, speex-5 0.52 versus soxr-vhq 0.25, soxr-hq 0.19. 96 kHz float to 44.1 kHz: speex-10 5.43 versus soxr-vhq 0.30. Top presets therefore about 15-18x faster (derived from page data); speex-5 versus soxr-hq about 2.7-3.5x (derived).
hardware: Core i7 2600K with 16 GiB RAM, Kubuntu 14.10 x86_64, soxr 0.1.1
tradeoffs: LGPL licence. soxr's quality presets add input delay of about 20 ms at HQ/VHQ in this page's delay table versus 0.17-2.9 ms for speex presets, so it suits offline or buffered conversion more than ultra-low-latency use.
caveats: Independent third-party comparison (Lastique/src_test, code and results published; last commit 2022-04-15), found as extra evidence for an already catalogued project. The data is from 2014 (soxr 0.1.1, speex 1.2rc1) so both libraries have moved on; compiler and flags are not stated; quality is compared by spectrograms, not matched quantitatively, so pairing speex-10 with soxr-vhq is approximate. The page's results are single runs per cell with no variance. libsoxr's own repo has no commits since 2018-02-24.
found_via: WebSearch 'audio resampler benchmark libsamplerate soxr speexdsp zita-resampler comparison speed github repository results table' (page lastique.github.io/src_test read via its gh-pages branch on raw.githubusercontent.com)
